In the older literature, there were just two kinds of incompatibilists—hard determinists and libertarians. A hard determinist is an incompatibilist who believes that determinism is in fact true (or, perhaps, that it is close enough to being true so far as we are concerned, in the ways relevant to free will) and because of this we lack free will (Holbach 1770; Wegner 2003). A libertarian is an incompatibilist who believes that we in fact have free will and this entails that determinism is false, in the right kind of way (van Inwagen 1983). Traditionally, libertarians have believed that “the right kind of way” requires that agents have a special and mysterious causal power not had by anything else in nature: a godlike power to be an uncaused cause of changes in the world (Chisholm 1964). Libertarians who hold this view are committed, it seems, to the claim that free will is possible only at worlds that are at least partly lawless, and that our world is such a world (but see O’Connor 2000, Clarke 2003 and Steward 2012). But in the contemporary literature there are incompatibilists who avoid such risky metaphysical claims by arguing that free will is possible at worlds where some of our actions have indeterministic event causes (Kane 1996, 1999, 2008, 2011a; Ekstrom 2000; Balaguer 2010; Franklin 2018) or that free will is possible at worlds where some of our actions are uncaused (Ginet 1990). Note that none of these three kinds of incompatibilists (agent-causation theorists, indeterministic event-causation theorists, non-causal theorists) need be libertarians. They may reserve judgment about the truth or falsity of determinism and therefore reserve judgment about whether or not we in fact have free will. They might also be hard determinists because they believe that determinism is in fact true.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. That's a very different kind of economics—and a more honest one.

Here's the simplest version:

---

**The Circular Argument Problem**

Economics textbooks say: "Capitalists deserve their profits because of how much capital they contribute."

Sounds reasonable. But Robinson asked: **How do you measure "how much capital" someone has?**

You can't just count machines—a factory robot and a sewing machine are different things. You need to add up their *value*. But what determines the value of a machine? The profits it can generate.

So the argument becomes:

- "Profits are determined by how much capital you have"
- "But how much capital you have is determined by... profits"

**That's circular.** You can't use profits to explain profits.

---

**A Kid-Friendly Analogy**

Imagine someone says: "I deserve a bigger slice of pizza because I brought more to the party."

You ask: "How do we know you brought more?"

They say: "Well, whatever I brought is worth however big a slice I end up getting."

That's not an explanation—it's just describing the outcome twice. The "because" is fake.

---

**Why It Matters**

The textbook story makes wages and profits seem like *technical facts*—determined by math and productivity, not by power or bargaining or history.

Robinson showed the math doesn't actually work. Which means the distribution of income is a *social* outcome, not a technical necessity. People could decide to divide things differently.

To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). ## Answer: Is Free Will Compatible with Determinism?

This question lies at the heart of one of philosophy's enduring debates. The answer depends on which position you take in a framework that has resisted consensus for centuries.

### The Main Positions (General Knowledge)

The debate divides into two primary camps:

**Compatibilists** argue *yes*, free will and determinism are compatible. They typically redefine "free will" not as freedom from causal determination, but rather as the ability to act according to one's own motivations without external coercion or constraint. Figures like David Hume, Daniel Dennett, and Harry Frankfurt have defended versions of this view.

**Incompatibilists** argue *no*, they cannot both be true simultaneously. This position further splits:
- **Hard determinism**: Determinism is true; therefore free will does not exist (or at least the kind required for moral responsibility)
- **Libertarianism** (metaphysical): Free will exists in a meaningful sense; therefore determinism must be false

### What the Sources Contribute

Compatibilism is explicitly defined as "the thesis that *free will* is compatible with *deterministim*" [Source: compatibilism]. This view is sometimes expressed equivalently regarding moral responsibility rather than free will directly, since freedom is typically taken to be a necessary condition for holding someone responsible.

Joan Robinson's economic theories

tined as "not the way we do things," you cannot develop alternatives at scale.

Robinson's constructive program may have been underdeveloped partly *because* the discipline's ideological commitments prevented serious engagement with it. The critique is dismissed for lacking a full alternative; the alternative remains undeveloped because the critique is dismissed. This circularity is how paradigms protect themselves.

## The Methodological Point Remains Unanswered

Robinson's deeper argument was about time and causation. Neoclassical equilibrium analysis treats the economy as a set of simultaneous equations—everything determined together, with no before and after. But actual economies unfold historically. Investment today depends on expectations formed yesterday about a future that hasn't happened. Capital equipment embodies past decisions that constrain present choices.

This isn't a technical quibble. It's a claim that equilibrium economics systematically misdescribes causation—that it can generate elegant models precisely because it abstracts from what matters: path-dependence, uncertainty, the irreversibility of time.

The discipline never answered this. It developed dynamic models, rational expectations, DSGE frameworks—but these still fundamentally treat time as a parameter in equations rather than as the medium of irreversible historical causation. Robinson would say they formalized time without understanding it.

## The Synthesis

So: Robinson was a prophet in that she identified genuine contradictions that the discipline acknowledged but refused to take seriously, which is what ideological capture looks like. And she was a critic whose negative program outran her constructive alternatives—but partly because the discipline's ideological closure prevented those alternatives from developing.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

When he arrived home to find his children arguing loudly and his wife looking exhausted, he recognized his own fatigue but chose to be present. "Let me take over dinner," he offered.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

The free will problem centers on whether human freedom is compatible with determinism—the view that all events, including decisions and actions, are causally inevitable [Source: Determinism]. Philosophers broadly divide into two camps regarding this relationship.

### Compatibilism
Compatibilism maintains that free will (and moral responsibility) is compatible even in a deterministic universe [Source: compatibilism]. Because free will is typically required for moral responsibility, compatibilists argue we can be morally responsible agents despite causal determination [Source: compatibilism]. 

*   **Historical roots:** Versions have existed since ancient times; notably, the Stoics like Chrysippus argued that while determinism is true, human actions aren't entirely explained by external factors, leaving room for praise and blame [Source: moral-responsibility]. In the modern period, philosophers like Hobbes and Hume distinguished between general necessity imposed by determinism and specific constraints (like physical impediments) placed on an agent's behavior [Source: moral-responsibility]. 
*   **Classical analysis:** Classical compatibilists analyzed free will conditionally. They asserted that to say an agent "could have done otherwise" means only that *if* they had chosen differently at that moment, they would have acted differently [Source: compatibilism]. Under this view, if a person acts according to their unimpeded wants—and those wants causally determine their actions—they act freely, even if the universe is deterministic [Source: compatibilism].
*   **Modern variations:** Modern compatibilists take different approaches. Some argue determinism doesn't threaten our freedom to do otherwise (e.g., Berofsky 1987; Vihvelin 2013) [Source: compatibilism]. Others reject the idea that "freedom to do otherwise" is necessary for free will at all, focusing instead on what Dennett calls the "varieties of free will worth wanting," such as reasons-responsiveness or Strawsonian reactive attitudes (Frankfurt 1969; Watson 1975; Fischer and Ravizza 1998) [Source: compatibilism][Web: incompatibilism-arguments]. 
*   **Computational perspectives:** Daniel Dennett and Stephen Wolfram have used cellular automata to argue determinism doesn't preclude freedom. Dennett uses high-level design stances to challenge inevitability, while Wolfram posits computational irreducibility as a scientific basis for compatibility [Source: cellular-automata][Web: cellular-automata].

### Incompatibilism
Incompatibilists hold that free will and causal determinism are mutually exclusive—meaning we only act freely if determinism is false [Source: incompatibilism-theories]. This camp includes both hard determinists (who claim determinism *is* true, therefore no free will) and metaphysical libertarians (who claim indeterminism must be true so free will can exist) [Source: Free will]. 

*   **Core argument:** The primary incompatibilist stance relies on the idea that genuine freedom requires a real ability to do otherwise. If the past or laws of nature are fixed, agents cannot possess the power to alter their actions without violating logical consistency [Web: incompatibilism-arguments]. Thought experiments like van Inwagen’s "No Forking Paths" illustrate this by showing how an agent might lack alternative possibilities if everything is causally predetermined [Web: incompatibilism-arguments].

Therefore, under hard incompatibilism, free will is impossible regardless of whether the universe is deterministic or indeterministic (a pessimistic view famously argued by C.D. Broad) [Source: Free will][Web: broad].

### Experimental Philosophy and Other Perspectives
Experimental philosophy reveals a fascinating nuance: people hold conflicting compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions simultaneously depending on how they frame determinism—viewing it as predictable causality tends to elicit compatibilist responses, while framing it as "mental bypassing" triggers incompatibilist reactions [Web: experimental-philosophy]. 

Additionally, some philosophical frameworks look beyond traditional causal models. For instance, cellular automata perspectives suggest that emergent behaviors in complex systems might offer new epistemological grounds for understanding agency without breaking physical laws [Source: cellular-automata][Web: cellular-automata]. Meanwhile, the debate remains deeply entangled with theological questions; classical compatiblists like Jonathan Edwards argued freedom is compatible even if determined by divine providence or factors within creation so long as those factors align with the agent's nature [Source: providence-divine].

Notably, thinkers like William James categorized these stances historically. He coined "hard determinism" (fatalistic and binding) versus "soft determinism"—the latter term now largely replaced by "compatibilism," which claims that recognizing necessity actually constitutes true freedom because bondage to higher causes is identical to rational liberty [Source: William James][Web: incompatibilism-arguments].

The free will/determinism problem centers on a fundamental dispute: are our choices genuinely ours, or are they the inevitable result of prior causes? The debate is primarily structured by two opposing stances—**compatibilism**, which holds that free will and determinism can coexist, and **incompatibilism**, which argues they cannot.

### Core Definitions
* **Determinism:** The view that all events in the universe, including human decisions and actions, are causally inevitable [Source: Determinism]. It suggests only one course of events is possible at any given moment [Source: Free will].
* **Compatibilism:** Defined as "the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism" or causal determinism [Source: compatibilism]. Because moral responsibility typically requires free will, compatibilists also argue for the compatibility between moral responsibility and a determined world [Source: William James; Source: compatibilism].
* **Incompatibilism:** Holds that we act freely *only if* determinism is false. Incompatibilists agree on this exclusion but disagree on what else is required (e.g., uncaused events vs. agent-caused events) [Source: incompatibilism-theories].

### The History of the Debate
The debate spans over two millennia. Ancient philosophers like Chrysippus argued that while actions are necessitated by external factors, they remain compatible with praise and blame because they stem from internal character rather than physical impediments [Source: moral-responsibility]. 

A major turning point occurred in 1884 when William James delivered his lecture *"The Dilemma of Determinism."* James defined "hard determinism" as the traditional view involving fatality and bondage of the will, whereas he labeled what we now call compatibilism as **"soft determinism"**—the idea that freedom is merely necessity understood properly [Source: William James].

### Key Arguments
**Incompatibilist arguments** often rely on the claim that true free will requires a genuine **ability to do otherwise**. If determinism is true, the past and laws of nature are fixed; thus, an agent cannot alter their actions without violating logical consistency.

**Compatibilist strategies** generally fall into two categories based on how they address the "ability to do otherwise":
1. **Conditional Analysis:** Classical compatibilists (like Hume) argued that an agent *could* have done otherwise if they had chosen differently. They analyzed free will in conditional terms rather than categorical ones—meaning a person is free as long as no external constraints prevent them from acting on their desires, even if those desires are determined [Source: compatibilism]. 
2. **Rejecting Alternative Possibilities:** Modern compatibilists argue that the ability to do otherwise isn't necessary for moral responsibility or meaningful agency. Figures like Daniel Dennett and John Martin Fischer suggest we only need **"reasons-responsiveness"** or Strawsonian reactive attitudes to be considered morally responsible agents [Web: incompatibilism-arguments; Web: compatibilism].

### Theological Determinism
The debate extends into theology with **theological determinism**. Some theologians adopt a libertarian view (claiming divine foreknowledge doesn't negate free will), while others embrace classical compatibilism—most famously Jonathan Edwards—who argued that freedom is compatible even when determined by causal factors within creation, provided those factors are of the "right sort" [Source: providence-divine].

### Experimental Philosophy & Modern Perspectives
Recent experimental philosophy suggests people naturally hold both compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions depending on how they frame determinism. When framed as predictable causality, people lean toward incompatibilism; when framed as mental bypassing or randomness, their views shift accordingly [Web: experimental-philosophy]. 

Modern thinkers like **Daniel Dennett** and **Stephen Wolfram** have also approached the problem through computational theory (specifically cellular automata). They argue that adopting a high-level design stance—viewing agents as complex systems capable of rational deliberation rather than just quantum particles—dissolves the mystery, showing free will is compatible with deterministic physical laws [Source: cellular-automata; Source: cellular-automata].

*   **Reasons-Responsiveness and Moral Agency:** Modern compatibilists (e.g., John Martin Fischer, Paul Russell) argue that free will requires a specific type of control—such as being responsive to reasons or satisfying Strawsonian reactive attitudes—rather than a metaphysical ability to break natural laws [Web: compatibilism]. They reject the idea that "freedom to do otherwise" in an indeterministic sense is necessary for meaningful agency [Source: compatibilism].
*   **Computational/Epistemic Stances:** Daniel Dennett and Stephen Wolfram have argued from cellular automata perspectives. Dennett uses high-level design stances to challenge notions of inevitability, while Wolfram posits computational irreducibility to suggest compatibility at a scientific level [Web: cellular-automata].

### 2. Incompatibilist Theories
Incompatibilists hold that if determinism is true, agents cannot act freely because they lack the power to alter their actions given the past and laws of nature [Web: incompatibilism-arguments]. They disagree on what form indeterminism must take (e.g., uncaused events vs. agent-caused events) where it occurs in action processes [Source: incompatibilism-theories]. Key theories include:

*   **Hard Determinism:** Asserts determinism is true; therefore, free will does not exist [Source: William James], [Source: Free will].
*   **Metaphysical Libertarianism:** Asserts free will exists; therefore, determinism is false [Source: Free will].
*   **Agent-Causal Accounts:** Propose that agents themselves are substances capable of initiating causal chains without being fully determined by prior physical states (associated with Chisholm and Pereboom) [Web: incompatibilism-theories].
*   **Event-Causal and Noncausal Accounts:** Various models attempt to ground agency in indeterministic events or non-causal facts while avoiding the "Problem of Luck" (the objection that if an action isn't caused/determined, it's just random/luck) [Web: incompatibilism-theories], [Source: incompatibilism-theories].

### 3. Key Fault Lines & Arguments
The debate is often framed around specific arguments and thought experiments:
*   **Consequence Argument & No Forking Paths:** Incompatibilists argue that because we cannot change the past or laws of nature, we have no power over their consequences; thus, we lack alternative possibilities [Web: incompatibilism-arguments].
*   **Frankfurt Cases:** Designed to defeat the Principle of Alternative Possibilities (the idea that you are only free if you could do otherwise), though these cases remain actively debated regarding "flicker-of-freedom" strategies [Source: Edgy Demos], [Web: broad].
*   **Historical Context:** William James famously categorized positions as hard determinism and soft/compatibilist determinism in 1884 [Source: William James]. Ancient Stoics like Chrysippus also argued early compatibilist views—that actions aren't entirely external, allowing for praise/blame even under necessity [Source: moral-responsibility].

### Unresolved Questions & Contested Points
*   **Luck Problem:** Incompatibilists must explain how agent-caused or event-caused indeterministic choices are any less "random" than luck, preserving genuine control (a major challenge to libertarian models) [Web: incompatibilism-theories].
*   **Experimental Philosophy Intuitions:** Research shows individuals hold conflicting intuitions based on framing—whether determinism is presented as predictable causality vs. mental bypassing suggests conceptual confusion may drive parts of the debate [Web: experimental-philosophy].
*   **Empirical Support for Indeterminism:** It remains debated whether quantum mechanics or subjective experience provides sufficient metaphysical grounding for non-deterministic agency without violating natural laws [Web: incompatibilism-theories].

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. The free will/determinism problem centers on a fundamental dispute: are our choices genuinely ours, or are they the inevitable result of prior causes? The debate is primarily structured by two opposing stances—**compatibilism**, which holds that free will and determinism can coexist, and **incompatibilism**, which argues they cannot.

### Core Definitions
*   **Determinism:** The view that all events in the universe, including human decisions and actions, are causally inevitable [Source: Determinism]. It suggests only one course of events is possible at any given moment [Source: Free will].
*   **Compatibilism:** Defined as "the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism" or causal determinism [Source: compatibilism]. Because moral responsibility typically requires free will, compatibilists also argue for the compatibility between moral responsibility and a determined world [Source: William James; Source: compatibilism].
*   **Incompatibilism:** Holds that we act freely *only if* determinism is false. Incompatibilists agree on this exclusion but disagree on what else is required (e.g., uncaused events vs. agent-caused events) [Source: incompatibilism-theories].

### The History of the Debate
The debate spans over two millennia. Ancient philosophers like Chrysippus argued that while actions are necessitated by external factors, they remain compatible with praise and blame because they stem from internal character rather than physical impediments [Source: moral-responsibility]. 

A major turning point occurred in 1884 when William James delivered his lecture *"The Dilemma of Determinism."* James defined "hard determinism" as the traditional view involving fatality and bondage of the will, whereas he labeled what we now call compatibilism as **"soft determinism"**—the idea that freedom is merely necessity understood properly [Source: William James].

### Key Arguments
**Incompatibilist arguments** often rely on the claim that true free will requires a genuine **ability to do otherwise**. If determinism is true, the past and laws of nature are fixed; thus, an agent cannot alter their actions without violating logical consistency. Incompatibilists use thought experiments like Peter van Inwagen's **No Forking Paths** (if you can't change the past or the laws of nature, you can't change your future actions) and **Frankfurt cases** to argue against this requirement or demonstrate its impossibility under determinism [Web: incompatibilism-arguments; Source: Edgy Demos].

**Compatibilist strategies** generally fall into two categories based on how they address the "ability to do otherwise":
1.  **Conditional Analysis:** Classical compatibilists (like Hume) argued that an agent *could* have done otherwise if they had chosen differently. They analyzed free will in conditional terms rather than categorical ones—meaning a person is free as long as no external constraints prevent them from acting on their desires, even if those desires are determined [Source: compatibilism]. 
2.  **Rejecting Alternative Possibilities:** Modern compatibilists argue that the ability to do otherwise isn't necessary for moral responsibility or meaningful agency. Figures like Daniel Dennett and John Martin Fischer suggest we only need **"reasons-responsiveness"** or Strawsonian reactive attitudes to be considered morally responsible agents [Web: incompatibilism-arguments; Web: compatibilism].

### Theological Determinism
The debate extends into theology with **theological determinism**. Some theologians adopt a libertarian view (claiming divine foreknowledge doesn't negate free will), while others embrace classical compatibilism—most famously Jonathan Edwards—who argued that freedom is compatible even when determined by causal factors within creation, provided those factors are of the "right sort" [Source: providence-divine].

### Experimental Philosophy & Modern Perspectives
Recent experimental philosophy suggests people naturally hold both compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions depending on how they frame determinism. When framed as predictable causality, people lean toward incompatibilism; when framed as mental bypassing or randomness, their views shift accordingly [Web: experimental-philosophy]. 

Modern thinkers like **Daniel Dennett** and **Stephen Wolfram** have also approached the problem through computational theory (specifically cellular automata). They argue that adopting a high-level design stance—viewing agents as complex systems capable of rational deliberation rather than just quantum particles—dissolves the mystery, showing free will is compatible with deterministic physical laws [Source: cellular-automata; Source: cellular-automata].

### Summary Table
| Position | Stance on Determinism | Core Argument for Free Will/Responsibility | Key Figures |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hard Determinism** | True & Incompatible | None exist. Actions are inevitable. | Historical determinists [Source: William James] |
| **Soft Determinism (Compatibilism)** | True & Compatible | Freedom = acting without external constraints / reasons-responsiveness. | Hume, Hobbes, Dennett, Edwards [Source: compatibilism; Source: providence-divine] |
| **Libertarianism** | False & Necessary | Agents possess a specific type of indeterminism to cause actions directly or indirectly. | Kane, Clarke [Web: incompatibilism-theories] |

The relationship between free will and determinism is the central fault line in this domain, dividing philosophers into **compatibilists** (who argue they are compatible) and **incompatibilists** (who argue they mutually exclude one another).

### 1. The Core Disagreement
*   **Compatibilism:** Defined as the thesis that free will—and by extension moral responsibility—is compatible with causal determinism [Source: compatibilism]. Proponents argue that even if a universe is deterministic, agents act freely so long as their actions flow from their own choices without external constraint [Source: moral-responsibility], or they reject the "ability to do otherwise" as a necessary condition for meaningful freedom [Source: compatibilism; Source: Web: broad].
*   **Incompatibilism:** Holds that because determinism implies only one course of events was possible given the past and laws of nature, it eliminates the genuine ability to act differently. Therefore, if determinism is true, free will does not exist [Source: incompatibilism-arguments]; Web: incompatibilism-theories). Incompatibilists are divided into those who believe indeterminism *is* required for free will (Libertarianism) and those who believe neither determinism nor indeterminism allows for free will (Hard Determinism / Hard Incompatibilism) [Source: Free will].

### 2. Historical Evolution and Key Figures
*   **Classical Compatibilism:** Early proponents like David Hume argued that freedom simply means acting according to one's own wants rather than being physically forced. They used "conditional analysis" to argue an agent could have done otherwise if they had chosen differently, even in a determined world [Source: compatibilism]. 
*   **William James:** Coined the terms "hard determinism" and "soft determinism" (now compatibilism), critiquing soft determinists for renaming necessity as freedom [Source: William James].
*   **Stoics & Locke:** Ancient Stoics like Chrysippus argued external determination does not negate internal agency; John Locke is frequently cited in modern debates regarding whether his specific framework aligns with classical or modern compatibilist views of causal chains [Source: moral-responsibility; Source: locke-freedom].

### 3. Modern Fault Lines
Modern debate has moved beyond simple definitions to specific metaphysical requirements for free will:
*   **The Ability to Do Otherwise:** Incompatabilists argue this ability is the "freedom requirement" for responsibility [Source: incompatibilism-arguments]. Compatibilists (like Robert Kane, though he bridges both sides) and reasons-responsive theorists like John Martin Fischer attempt to redefine control so it doesn't strictly require alternative possibilities in a deterministic timeline [Web: broad]. 
*   **Agent-Causation vs Event-Causation:** A major divide among incompatibilists concerns *where* indeterminism must occur. Does an agent need to be a unique causal substance that initiates events without prior causes? Or are standard event-causal chains sufficient if they aren't fully determined by external factors? Theories struggle with the "problem of luck"—if an action isn't caused by the agent's character or prior state (due to randomness), can we still hold them responsible for it? [Source: incompatibilism-theories; Source: experimental-philosophy]

### 4. Empirical and Computational Perspectives
*   **Experimental Philosophy:** Research suggests people naturally oscillate between compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions depending on how determinism is framed—e.g., viewing it as predictable causality versus a bypassing of mental processes [Web: experimental-philosophy]. 
*   **Computational Models & Cellular Automata:** Modern thinkers like Daniel Dennett use cellular automata models as "intuition pumps" to demonstrate that complex, deterministic systems (like brains) can exhibit behavior indistinguishable from free agency when viewed through the right epistemological lens. Stephen Wolfram similarly uses computational irreducibility to argue for compatibility [Source: cellular-automata; Source: Web: broad].

### Unresolved Questions
The debate remains active because no side has definitively solved the "problem of luck" or provided empirical proof regarding whether human decision-making is fundamentally causal and determined or truly open-ended [Source: incompatibilism-theories].

The free will/determinism problem centers on whether human agents can possess free will if every event, including decisions and actions, is causally inevitable. The debate splits into two primary camps: **compatibilism** (free will is compatible with determinism) and **incompatibilism** (they are mutually exclusive).

### 1. Incompatibilism
Incompatibilists argue that for an agent to act freely, the future must not be fixed by past events or laws of nature [Source: incompatibilism-arguments]. If determinism were true, we would lack the "genuine ability to do otherwise," which they consider a necessary condition for moral responsibility [Source: incompatibilism-arguments; Source: Web: broad]. This camp includes:
*   **Hard Determinism:** The view that determinism is true, meaning free will is impossible [Source: Free will; Source: William James].
*   **Metaphysical Libertarianism:** The view that indeterminism allows for genuine alternative possibilities and free will [Source: Free will].
*   **Hard Incompatibilism:** A position holding that both determinism *and* indeterminism are incompatible with free will—meaning free will is impossible regardless of how the universe operates (deterministic or random) [Source: Free will]. C.D. Broad represents a pessimist version of this by rejecting deterministic necessity while also finding no viable form of indeterminism to support agency [Web: broad].

Incompatibilists disagree among themselves on what type of indeterminism would be required if it existed (e.g., uncaused events, nondeterministically caused events, or agent-caused events), and where in an action's process such indeterminism must occur [Source: incompatibilism-theories]. Theoretical models include noncausal, event-causal, and agent-causal accounts [Web: incompatinar-theories], though these face the "problem of luck"—the objection that random events do not constitute responsible agency. Incompatiblists often use thought experiments like van Inwagen’s No Forking Paths and Frankfurt cases to argue that a fixed past eliminates alternative possibilities [Source: Web: incompatinar-arguments].

### 2. Compatibilism
Compatibilists maintain that free will (and moral responsibility) is compatible with causal determinism because freedom does not require an uncaused ability to alter the past or laws of nature. Instead, it requires acting without external constraints in accordance with one's own desires and choices [Source: compatibilism; Source: moral-responsibility]. 
*   **Classical Compatibilism:** Figures such as Thomas Hobbes and David Hume distinguished between internal psychological necessity and external coercion (e.g., physical imprisonment). They argued that even if actions are causally determined by an agent's character, they remain "free" so long as the agent acts on what they want to do [Source: moral-responsibility; Source: William James]. Classical compatibilists often analyzed the ability to "do otherwise" conditionally—meaning an agent could have done otherwise *if* they had willed it differently [Source: compatibilism].
*   **Modern/Strawsonian Approaches:** Contemporary compatibilists like John Martin Fischer advance ideas such as "reasons-responsiveness," arguing that control is about being responsive to rational reasons rather than having access to alternative physical possibilities. Others adopt a Strawsonian approach or reject the necessity of alternative possibilities altogether, focusing instead on whether actions flow from the agent's own will (e.g., Daniel Dennett) [Web: compatilarism; Source: compatilarism].

### 3. Historical and Conceptual Evolution
The terminology has shifted over time. William James noted in his 1884 lecture "The Dilemma of Determinism" that older philosophers used terms like "hard determinism" for fatalistic views, while "soft determinism"—a term largely abandoned today—was what modern philosophy now calls **compatibilism** [Source: William James]. 

Ancient Greek thinkers first identified this tension, which remains a major focus of debate. The Stoic Chrysippus argued early on that determined actions are not necessarily explained by external factors, preserving room for praise and blame [Source: moral-responsibility]. In contemporary physics-inspired debates, Daniel Dennett and Stephen Wolfram have utilized cellular automata to argue that high-level computational or design stances allow free will to coexist with deterministic systems, whereas critics question whether such emergent properties constitute genuine freedom [Source: cellular-automata; Source: cellular-automata].

### Unresolved Tensions
*   **The Problem of Luck:** If an action depends partly on random (indeterministic) events, can the agent truly be responsible for it? This remains a central objection raised against libertarian theories by philosophers like Robert Kane and Derk Pereboom [Web: incompatinar-theories]. 
*   **Empirical vs. Metaphysical:** Incompatibilist theories debate whether empirical evidence from quantum mechanics or subjective human experience provides grounds for metaphysical indeterminism in agency [Web: incompatiar-theories].
*   **Experimental Philosophy:** Recent studies indicate that ordinary people hold both compatibilist and incompatibilist intuitions simultaneously—shifting between them depending on how determinism is framed (e.g., as predictable causality versus "mental bypassing") [Web: experimental-philosophy; Source: Web: experimental-philosophy].

The free will/determinism problem centers on whether humans can act freely if every event is causally inevitable. The debate splits primarily into **compatibilism** and **incompatibilism**, with significant internal subdivisions within both camps regarding moral responsibility, the nature of "ability," and the role of indeterminism [Source: compatibilism; Source: incompatibilism-arguments].

### 1. Core Definitions
* **Determinism:** The view that all events in the universe, including human decisions, are causally inevitable given prior states and natural laws [Source: Determinism]. Hard determinists argue this means free will is impossible [Source: Free will].
* **Compatibilism ("Soft Determinism"):** The thesis that free will (and moral responsibility) is compatible with causal determinism [Source: compatibilism]. John Maynard Keynes’ contemporary, William James, termed this "soft determinism," noting its preference for terms like "freedom" over "necessity or fatality" [Source: William James]. 
* **Incompatibilism:** The view that free will and determinism are mutually exclusive. This includes *hard incompatibilism*, which claims even indeterminism fails to provide the kind of freedom required for agency [Source: Free will; Source: incompatibilism-theories].

### 2. Compatibilist Strategies
Compatibilists generally argue that determinism does not undermine our status as morally responsible agents through several distinct strategies [Source: compatibilism]:
* **Conditional Analysis (Classical):** Philosophers such as David Hume, A.J. Ayer, and Hobart analyzed an agent’s "ability to do otherwise" in conditional terms. They argued that saying an agent *could have done Y* simply means they *would have done Y* had they chosen/willed it at the time [Source: compatibilism]. 
* **Reasons-Responsiveness:** Figures like John Martin Fischer reject the necessity of the freedom to do otherwise entirely. Instead, they argue moral responsibility requires only that an agent's actions are responsive to reasons [Web: compatibilism].
* **Strawsonian/Attitudinal Approaches:** Thinkers such as Paul Russell focus on reactive attitudes (e.g., blame and praise) rather than metaphysical "power" over events [Web: compatabilism; Source: compatibilism].
* **Cellular Automata & Computation:** Modern thinkers like Daniel Dennett and Stephen Wolfram use cellular automata to dissolve the free will mystery. They suggest adopting a high-level "design stance"—where computational irreducibility or complex emergent behavior makes the illusion of choice functionally equivalent to genuine agency, challenging notions of inevitability without requiring indeterminism [Source: cellular-automata; Source: cellular-automata].

### 3. 
* **The Problem of Luck:** If an action is undetermined due to randomness, critics argue its occurrence is a matter of luck rather than controlled by the agent [Web: incompatibilism-theories].
* **Agent-Causal vs. Event-Causal:** To solve this, theorists like Robert Kane and Roderick Chisholm propose "agent-causal" accounts—where agents themselves are fundamental substances that cause events without being fully determined by prior natural laws [Web: incompatibilism-theories; Source: incompatibilism-theories]. Others rely on event-causal models or noncausal theories (e.g., Clarke) but must explain how these avoid violating physical laws while maintaining control [Web: incompatibilism-theories].

### 4. Historical & Theological Context
* **Ancient/Modern Roots:** Stoics such as Chrysippus argued determinism does not necessitate external compulsion, allowing for internal choice compatible with praise/blame [Source: moral-responsibility]. Thomas Hobbes and David Hume later distinguished general causal necessity from specific everyday constraints like physical imprisonment [Source: compatibilism; Source: moral-responsibility]. John Locke is often analyzed through this lens of distinguishing the *nature* of determination from external coercion [Source: locke-freedom].
* **Theological Determinism:** Jonathan Edwards famously defended a classically compatibilist view where freedom is compatible even with divine or created-order causation, provided the causal factors are "of the right sort" (i.e., aligning with one's desires) [Source: providence-divine].

### 5. Unresolved Questions & Open Fronts
Despite millennia of debate, several areas remain actively contested and unresolved in contemporary literature:
1. **Frankfurt Cases vs. PAP:** Whether Frankfurt-style cases successfully defeat the Principle of Alternative Possibilities remains an open front alongside the "timing objection" and "flicker-of-freedom strategy" [Source: Edgy Demos; Source: compatibilism]. 
2. **Empirical Evidence for Indeterminism:** Incompatibilists frequently appeal to quantum mechanics or subjective experience to prove indeterministic agency exists, but whether these scientific/phenomenological facts actually satisfy metaphysical requirements is heavily debated [Web: incompatibilism-theories].
3. **Experimental Philosophy Discrepancies:** Experimental philosophy reveals that individuals hold *conflicting* compatibilist/incompatibilist intuitions depending on how determinism is framed (e.g., predictable causality vs. "mental bypassing"). Scholars debate whether this fluctuation stems from conceptual errors, linguistic usage, or deep moral influence [Source: experimental-philosophy; Source: experimental-philosophy].

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. [System response — a structured debate map:]

POSITIONS:

Hard Determinism All events are causally determined. Free will is an illusion. Moral responsibility requires revision. [SEP §3.1, citing Pereboom, Smilansky]

Compatibilism Determinism and free will are compatible. Freedom means acting according to one's own desires without external constraint, not the ability to have done otherwise. [SEP §4, citing Frankfurt, Dennett, Wolf]

Libertarianism (metaphysical) Some actions are genuinely undetermined. Agent causation provides the ground for free will. [SEP §5, citing Kane, O'Connor, Clarke]

KEY TENSIONS:

1. The Consequence Argument (van Inwagen): If determinism is true, our actions are consequences of laws of nature and events before our birth. We have no control over those. Therefore we have no control over our actions. Compatibilists must answer this — Frankfurt cases are the primary response.
    
2. The Luck Objection (Mele): If an action is undetermined, then whether it occurs is a matter of luck. How can a lucky outcome ground moral responsibility? Libertarians must answer this.
    
3. The Manipulation Argument (Pereboom): If a manipulated agent isn't responsible, and there's no principled difference between manipulation and deterministic causation, then determined agents aren't responsible either. Compatibilists dispute the "no principled difference" step.

assume for the present—until next year—that it is no illusion. My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.

In 1884, James set the terms for all future discussions of determinism and compatibilism in the free will debates with his lecture to Harvard Divinity School students published as "The Dilemma of Determinism". In this talk he defined the common terms hard determinism and soft determinism (now more commonly called compatibilism).

Old-fashioned determinism was what we may call hard determinism. It did not shrink from such words as fatality, bondage of the will, necessitation, and the like. Nowadays, we have a soft determinism which abhors harsh words, and, repudiating fatality, necessity, and even predetermination, says that its real name is freedom; for freedom is only necessity understood, and bondage to the highest is identical with true freedom.

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. It was a marine chronometer of the old proud kind, brass-bound in a case of black walnut, made by the firm of Lyle & Hannett whose name was engraved across its face in letters like a ship's transom. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. It was a marine chronometer of the old proud kind, brass-bound in a case of black walnut, made by the firm of Lyle & Hannett whose name was engraved across its face in letters like a ship's transom. It had come off a wrecked Indiaman sixty years before, had been bought at the salvage auction by the village trust, and had hung on the office wall ever since as the official timepiece of the port of Glasswater Stave. Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

Now the walnut case hung open and the chronometer was gone, and the dust on the shelf below showed the clean square where its travelling box had stood.

A Tale of Glasswater Stave

CHAPTER I

The lock basin at Glasswater Stave held its water the way the village held its opinions: behind heavy gates, and grudgingly. At slack water on a grey morning the basin was a rectangle of pewter, walled in dressed stone, crossed by the shadows of mooring posts, and smelling of weed and tar and the cold iron of the sluice machinery. It was Tabb Orrison who found the harbormaster floating in it, a little after dawn, while the gulls were still arguing over the fish-gutting boards on the quay.

Tabb was the lock-keeper's apprentice, seventeen years old and not yet used to the idea that the sea kept no appointments. He had come down to grease the pawls of the eastern gate, as he did every third morning, and he saw first the harbormaster's coat — a good drab coat with horn buttons, spread on the water like a chart of some unlucky coast — and then the white hair, and then the face. He did not shout at once. He told Constable Marlock afterwards that the silence of it had seemed to forbid shouting, that the basin at slack water was like a church with the sexton drowned in the font. Then the cold sense of things returned to him and he ran up the quay yelling for help with his grease-can still in one hand.

Corwin Pellow had been harbormaster of Glasswater Stave for twenty-one years. He had a square, patient face, a habit of writing everything down, and a reputation along the whole Hethering coast for being un-bribable, which in a salvage port is a reputation with enemies attached to it. The village brought him out of the basin with a pair of gaffs and laid him on the weighing platform by the fish scales, and by seven o'clock the whole of Glasswater Stave knew that the harbormaster was drowned, and by half past seven the whole village had privately decided it was no accident, though nobody would say so above a whisper until the doctor had had his look.

CHAPTER IV

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. It was a marine chronometer of the old proud kind, brass-bound in a case of black walnut, made by the firm of Lyle & Hannett whose name was engraved across its face in letters like a ship's transom. It had come off a wrecked Indiaman sixty years before, had been bought at the salvage auction by the village trust, and had hung on the office wall ever since as the official timepiece of the port of Glasswater Stave. Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

Now the walnut case hung open and the chronometer was gone, and the dust on the shelf below showed the clean square where its travelling box had stood.

"Thieves, then," said Constable Marlock, writing in his notebook. "He surprised a thief at the office, and was struck, and put in the basin."

"Then the thief," said Maren, "knew enough to take the travelling box, which was kept in the cupboard, and to take the winding key, which was kept in the desk; and knew nothing about the cash drawer, which was not even locked. That is a thief with strange priorities, Constable."

They took Severin Quenholt at The Cold Lantern that evening, where he sat at his usual table with his usual glass, agreeing pleasantly with his neighbors about the sad state of the times.

He denied nothing for long; that was the strangest part, the village said afterwards, and the part that made it believable. Confronted in the inn's back parlor with the chronometer, the tobacco-tin accounts, the boat-hook stamped M.B., and the doctor's saucer of violet-blooming ink, he sat quiet for a while with his hands folded, like a merchant checking a column twice, and then he balanced the books aloud.

He had gone to the harbor office late on the fourteenth to reason with Pellow, he said — only to reason, to offer the survey a percentage of its own. CHAPTER VII

The inquest on Corwin Pellow was held on the third day, in the long room of The Cold Lantern, because the village had no other room that would hold the crowd. The coroner came out from Saltern Cross; the jury were seven men and two women of the village, sworn on the inn's own Bible with the fish-scale still under their nails; and Widow Hetch shut the bar for the duration, which the older men counted the most serious mark of the occasion.

Tabb Orrison gave his evidence first, twisting his cap, and was treated gently. He told how he had come down at first light to grease the pawls of the eastern gate; how he had seen the coat on the water and then the white hair; how he had run up the quay shouting with the grease-can still in his hand. Asked by the coroner whether the basin had shown anything else amiss, he said the water had stood high on the gauge for the time of month, which he had thought strange even in his fright, the tides then being at the neaps, and the gates shut fast since the Saltwillow came through on the evening of the fourteenth.

Doctor Imbrey Fosk gave the medical evidence in the dry, complete manner of long practice, and the long room was silent under it. Death by drowning, the lungs taking water, the man alive when he entered the basin. A wound at the right temple, got before the water: narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged, made by an iron edge swung with force, and not to be had from any fall against rounded and weeded coping stones. A man so struck, said the doctor, might be insensible past saving himself in two feet of water, let alone the basin's twelve.

The coroner asked whether the wound could have been self-got, and the doctor said that a man may do many things, but he does not commonly strike himself above the ear with an iron edge and then arrange to drown.

The registrar, called briefly, confirmed the heights of water in her ledger for the fourteenth and was not asked about its pages further, the constable having requested, in the interest of an inquiry then proceeding, that the documents not be canvassed in open court; and the coroner, an old hand, led the questions elsewhere.

The jury were out twenty minutes and returned the only verdict the evidence allowed: wilful murder, by a person or persons unknown. The coroner adjourned the inquest sine die, released the body for burial, and was driven back over the downs before dark. The Cold Lantern reopened its bar within the hour, and the long room, which had heard the word murder said aloud at last, said it over to itself all evening in every corner, quietly, the way the sea works at a stone.

CHAPTER VIII

Wrack Point light stood three miles east of the village on a shoulder of black rock, and Lessa Pellow kept it. ## What Philosophers Say About Compatibility

**Compatibilism directly affirms compatibility.** As noted in the Stanford Encyclopedia, "compatibilism is the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism" [Source: compatibilism]. Compatibilists argue that freedom consists not in being uncaused, but in acting according to one's own desires and reasons without external coercion.

**Incompatibilists deny compatibility.** Incompatibilist arguments hold that "having free will depends on a contingent fact about the laws that govern the universe: that they are indeterministic" [Source: incompatibilism-articles]. This position splits further into hard determinists (who believe we lack freedom) and libertarians (who argue for genuine alternative possibilities).

## Why There Is No Single Answer

The question "is free will compatible?" actually contains a deeper disagreement about what *free will* means. Compatibilists define it in ways that allow compatibility; incompatibilists require something stronger—genuine metaphysical openness to alternatives—that seems incompatible with determinism.

Compatibilists maintain that free will (and/or moral responsibility) is possible even in a deterministic universe. Versions of compatibilism have been defended since ancient times. For example, the Stoics—Chryssipus, in particular—argued that the truth of determinism does not entail that human actions are entirely explained by factors external to agents; thus, human actions are not necessarily explained in a way that is incompatible with praise and blame (see Bobzien 1998 and Salles 2005 for Stoic views on freedom and determinism). The difference is that the necessity involved in determinism is compatible with agents acting as they choose to act: even if S’s behavior is causally determined, it may be behavior that she chooses to perform. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). The view that posits free will as incompatible with determinism is called incompatibilism and encompasses both metaphysical libertarianism and hard determinism. Another incompatibilist position is hard incompatibilism, which holds not only determinism but also indeterminism to be incompatible with free will and thus free will to be impossible whatever the case may be regarding determinism. In contrast, compatibilists hold that free will is compatible with determinism. Some compatibilists even hold that determinism is necessary for free will, arguing that choice involves preference for one course of action over another, requiring a sense of how choices will turn out. Compatibilists thus consider the debate between libertarians and hard determinists over free will vs. determinism a false dilemma. Different compatibilists offer very different definitions of what "free will" means and consequently find different types of constraints to be relevant to the issue.

Free will

Incompatibilism is the position that free will and determinism are logically incompatible, and that the major question regarding whether or not people have free will is thus whether or not their actions are determined. "Hard determinists", such as d'Holbach, are those incompatibilists who accept determinism and reject free will. In contrast, " metaphysical libertarians ", such as Thomas Reid, Peter van Inwagen, and Robert Kane, are those incompatibilists who accept free will and deny determinism, holding the view that some form of indeterminism is true. Another view is that of hard incompatibilists, which state that free will is incompatible with both determinism and indeterminism.

Free will

To be a compatibilist, one need not endorse any particular conception of free will, but only deny that determinism is at odds with free will.

Determinism

due to chance. Determinism is often contrasted with free will, although some philosophers claim that the two are compatible.

Historically, debates about determinism have involved many philosophical positions and given rise to multiple varieties or interpretations of determinism. One topic of debate concerns the scope of determined systems. Some philosophers have maintained that the entire universe is a single determinate system, while others identify more limited determinate systems. Another common debate topic is whether determinism and free will can coexist; compatibilism and incompatibilism represent the opposing sides of this debate.

The denial of libertarian freedom has always had many supporters. The idea of making causal determinism the focal point of discussions of free will is modern in origin, and some philosophers think that the modern framing of the issue is confused. Philosophers who deny libertarian freedom may affirm a type of free will compatible with determinism, or they may instead simply accept the consequence that human beings lack free will. It is worth noting, however, that theists who deny libertarian freedom are typically theological determinists rather than fatalists; it’s primarily considerations of divine omnipotence or sovereignty, rather than foreknowledge, that motivate them. Jonathan Edwards, on the other hand, based his Calvinist denial of libertarian freedom, in part, on a sophisticated version of the argument for theological fatalism (FW II.12).

This question lies at the heart of one of philosophy's oldest and most contested debates. The retrieved sources frame how philosophers understand it [Source: freewill].

## What Philosophers Say About Compatibility

**Compatibilism directly affirms compatibility.** As noted in the Stanford Encyclopedia, "compatibilism is the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism" [Source: compatibilism]. Compatibilists argue that freedom consists not in being uncaused, but in acting according to one's own desires and reasons without external coercion.

**Incompatibilists deny compatibility.** Incompatibilist arguments hold that "having free will depends on a contingent fact about the laws that govern the universe: that they are indeterministic" [Source: incompatibilism-articles]. This position splits further into hard determinists (who believe we lack freedom) and libertarians (who argue for genuine alternative possibilities).

## Why There Is No Single Answer

The question "is free will compatible?" actually contains a deeper disagreement about what *free will* means. Compatibilists define it in ways that allow compatibility; incompatibilists require something stronger—genuine metaphysical openness to alternatives—that seems incompatible with determinism.

Incompatibilists hold that free will and determinism are mutually exclusive and, consequently, that we act freely (i.e., with free will) only if determinism is false. However, they disagree amongst themselves about what else, besides indeterminism, is required for free will. One question that divides them concerns which type of indeterminism—uncaused events, nondeterministically caused events, or agent caused events—is required. Another concerns where in the processes leading to action indeterminism must be located in order for an action to be free. Different answers to these questions yield different incompatibilist theories of free will.

So far it has been argued that theological determinism, by virtue of the nature of the determination involved (which may yield the result that it is even misleading to describe it as determination at all), may well be compatible with a basically libertarian view of free will. An alternative for proponents of theological determinism is to accept a classically compatibilist view of free will, according to which freedom is compatible even with determination by causal factors within the created order, so long as those causal factors are of the right sort. The most famous proponent of such a view is Jonathan Edwards, and such views are common in the contemporary free will literature. This discussion will proceed by focusing on the libertarian view of the will, but many of the same approaches can be taken by the compatibilist as well.

moral-responsibility

Compatibilists maintain that free will (and/or moral responsibility) is possible even in a deterministic universe. Versions of compatibilism have been defended since ancient times. For example, the Stoics—Chryssipus, in particular—argued that the truth of determinism does not entail that human actions are entirely explained by factors external to agents; thus, human actions are not necessarily explained in a way that is incompatible with praise and blame (see Bobzien 1998 and Salles 2005 for Stoic views on freedom and determinism). Similarly, philosophers in the Modern period (such as Hobbes and Hume) distinguished the general way in which our actions are necessitated if determinism is true from the specific instances of necessity sometimes imposed on us by everyday constraints on our behavior (e.g., physical impediments that make it impossible to act as we choose). The difference is that the necessity involved in determinism is compatible with agents acting as they choose to act: even if S’s behavior is causally determined, it may be behavior that she chooses to perform. And perhaps the ability that matters for free will (and responsibility) is just the ability to act as one chooses, which seems to require only the absence of external constraints (and not the absence of determinism).

Compatibilists, on the other hand, claim that these concerns miss the mark. Some compatibilists hold this because they think the truth of causal determinism would not undermine our freedom to do otherwise (Berofsky 1987, Campbell 1997, Vihvelin 2013, etc.). As a result, these compatibilists tell us, the truth of causal determinism poses no threat to our status as morally responsible agents (notice the enthymematic premise here: the freedom to do otherwise is sufficient for the kind of control an agent must possess to be morally responsible for her actions). Other compatibilists show less concern in rebutting the conclusion that the freedom to do otherwise is incompatible with determinism. Compatibilists of this stripe reject the idea that such freedom is necessary for meaningful forms of free will (e.g., Frankfurt 1969, 1971; Watson 1975, Dennett 1984)—the “varieties of free will worth wanting,” (Dennett 1984). And even more notably, some compatibilists simply deny that freedom of this sort is in any way connected to morally responsible agency (e.g., Fischer 1994, Fischer & Ravizza 1998, Scanlon 1998, Wallace 1994, Sartorio 2016). What we see here is not a unified front in the face of the incompatibilist challenge(s).  Instead, compatibilists have been careful to identify the precise elements of incompatibilists’ arguments that they take to be erroneous, and then build their respective theories of freedom and responsibility with that in mind.

If determinism is true, and if at any given time, an unimpeded agent is completely determined to have the wants that she does have, and if those wants causally determine her actions, then, even though she does do what she wants to do, she cannot ever do otherwise. She satisfies the classical compatibilist conditions for free will. But free will requires the ability to do otherwise, and determinism is incompatible with this. Hence, the classical compatibilist account of free will is inadequate. Determinism is incompatible with free will and moral responsibility because determinism is incompatible with the ability to do otherwise.

compatibilism

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Five demos. Each one is reproducible in under 30 minutes of setup on a MacBook with an 8B model. Each one is showable in a 3-minute video. Each one makes someone want to share it.

The principle: **pick questions people are already arguing about, and show the system mapping the argument instead of picking a side.** The system's neutrality is the superpower.

---

She satisfies the classical compatibilist conditions for free will. But free will requires the ability to do otherwise, and determinism is incompatible with this. compatibilism

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

The denial of libertarian freedom has always had many supporters. ## What Philosophers Say About Compatibility

**Compatibilism directly affirms compatibility.** As noted in the Stanford Encyclopedia, "compatibilism is the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism" [Source: compatibilism]. Compatibilists argue that freedom consists not in being uncaused, but in acting according to one's own desires and reasons without external coercion.

**Incompatibilists deny compatibility.** Incompatibilist arguments hold that "having free will depends on a contingent fact about the laws that govern the universe: that they are indeterministic" [Source: incompatibilism-articles]. This position splits further into hard determinists (who believe we lack freedom) and libertarians (who argue for genuine alternative possibilities).

## Why There Is No Single Answer

The question "is free will compatible?" actually contains a deeper disagreement about what *free will* means. Compatibilists define it in ways that allow compatibility; incompatibilists require something stronger—genuine metaphysical openness to alternatives—that seems incompatible with determinism.

However, they disagree amongst themselves about what else, besides indeterminism, is required for free will. So far it has been argued that theological determinism, by virtue of the nature of the determination involved (which may yield the result that it is even misleading to describe it as determination at all), may well be compatible with a basically libertarian view of free will. Compatibilists maintain that free will (and/or moral responsibility) is possible even in a deterministic universe. Versions of compatibilism have been defended since ancient times. For example, the Stoics—Chryssipus, in particular—argued that the truth of determinism does not entail that human actions are entirely explained by factors external to agents; thus, human actions are not necessarily explained in a way that is incompatible with praise and blame (see Bobzien 1998 and Salles 2005 for Stoic views on freedom and determinism). Similarly, philosophers in the Modern period (such as Hobbes and Hume) distinguished the general way in which our actions are necessitated if determinism is true from the specific instances of necessity sometimes imposed on us by everyday constraints on our behavior (e.g., physical impediments that make it impossible to act as we choose). The difference is that the necessity involved in determinism is compatible with agents acting as they choose to act: even if S’s behavior is causally determined, it may be behavior that she chooses to perform. And perhaps the ability that matters for free will (and responsibility) is just the ability to act as one chooses, which seems to require only the absence of external constraints (and not the absence of determinism).

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.

Classical compatibilists have responded by arguing that determinism is compatible with the ability to do otherwise. To show this, they attempted to analyze an agent’s ability to do otherwise in conditional terms (e.g., Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, p.73; Ayer 1954; or Hobart 1934). Since determinism is a thesis about what must happen in the future given the actual past, determinism is consistent with the future being different given a different past. So the classical compatibilists analyzed any assertion that an agent could have done otherwise as a conditional assertion reporting what an agent would have done under certain counterfactual conditions. These conditions involved variations on what a freely willing agent wanted (chose, willed, or decided) to do at the time of her freely willed action. Suppose that an agent freely willed X. According to the classical compatibilist conditional analysis, to say that, at the time of acting, she could have done Y and not X is just to say that, had she wanted (chosen, willed, or decided) to do Y and not X at that time, then she would have done Y and not done X. Her ability to have done otherwise at the time at which she acted consisted in some such counterfactual truth.
